content:
# The International Workingmen's Association, Resolution on the Procedure of Discussing the Programme of the Congress

The Congress of the International Workingmen's Association is a significant event that brings together representatives from various countries to discuss and formulate strategies for the advancement of the working class. 

In order to ensure a productive and efficient discussion, it is essential to establish clear procedures that will guide the deliberations. 

## Objectives of the Congress

The primary objectives of the Congress are to:

1. Assess the current state of the working class movement across different nations.
2. Identify common challenges faced by workers globally.
3. Develop a unified approach to address these challenges.

## Discussion Procedures

To facilitate a constructive dialogue, the following procedures shall be adopted:

1. **Preparation of Documents**: All delegates are required to submit their proposals and documents in advance. This will allow for thorough review and consideration prior to the Congress.

2. **Time Allocation**: Each speaker will be allotted a specific amount of time to present their views. This will ensure that all voices are heard and that discussions remain focused.

3. **Moderation**: A designated moderator will oversee the discussions to maintain order and ensure adherence to the established time limits.

4. **Voting Procedures**: Decisions will be made through a democratic voting process, allowing all delegates to express their support or opposition to proposals.

## Conclusion

The successful execution of the Congress relies on the active participation of all delegates and adherence to the established procedures. 

By fostering an environment of collaboration and respect, the International Workingmen's Association can effectively advance the interests of the working class and promote solidarity among workers worldwide.

title: The International Workingmen's Association, A warning
author: Karl Marx
description: The International Workingmen's Association, A warning by Karl Marx. Source: Marxists Internet Archive.

chapters.title: The International Workingmen's Association, A Warning

content:
# The International Workingmen's Association, A Warning

The International Workingmen's Association, founded in 1864, represents a significant milestone in the history of the labor movement. It was established to unite various labor organizations and promote the interests of the working class on an international scale. However, it is crucial to recognize the challenges and dangers that accompany such a movement.

## The Threat of Division

One of the primary threats to the unity of the working class is the potential for division among its ranks. The bourgeoisie will always attempt to exploit differences in nationality, language, and culture to weaken the solidarity of workers. It is essential for the International Workingmen's Association to remain vigilant against these divisive tactics.

The working class must understand that their struggles are interconnected. The fight for better wages, working conditions, and rights is not confined to one nation or region. It is a global struggle that requires a united front.

## The Role of Leadership

Leadership within the International Workingmen's Association plays a critical role in guiding the movement. It is imperative that leaders are committed to the principles of socialism and the emancipation of the working class. They must prioritize the needs of the workers over personal ambitions or political power.

Leaders should also foster an environment of inclusivity and collaboration among different labor organizations. This will strengthen the movement and ensure that all voices are heard.

## The Importance of Education

Education is a vital component of the labor movement. Workers must be informed about their rights, the nature of capitalism, and the principles of socialism. The International Workingmen's Association should prioritize educational initiatives to empower workers and equip them with the knowledge necessary to challenge the status quo.

By promoting education, the movement can cultivate a politically conscious working class that is capable of organizing and advocating for its interests.

## Conclusion

The International Workingmen's Association stands as a beacon of hope for the working class. However, it is essential to remain aware of the challenges that lie ahead. Unity, strong leadership, and education are crucial for the success of the movement. Only through collective action and solidarity can the working class achieve its goals and secure a better future for all.

content:
# The International Workingmen's Association

## Address from the Working Men's International Association to President Johnson (1865)

To His Excellency, Andrew Johnson, President of the United States of America:

The Working Men's International Association, representing the interests of the working class across the globe, addresses you with the utmost respect and earnestness. We are compelled to express our solidarity with the laboring masses of your nation and to convey our hopes for a just and equitable society.

The struggle for emancipation has reached a pivotal moment. The abolition of slavery in the United States marks a significant victory for human rights and dignity. It is a triumph not only for the American people but for all oppressed individuals worldwide. We recognize the sacrifices made by countless individuals who fought for this cause, and we honor their memory.

However, the end of slavery is merely the beginning of a larger struggle. The true liberation of the working class requires the dismantling of the capitalist structures that perpetuate inequality and exploitation. We urge you, as the leader of a nation that has taken a bold step towards freedom, to champion the rights of all workers. 

The working class must be empowered to participate fully in the political and economic life of the nation. This entails not only the right to vote but also the right to fair wages, safe working conditions, and the ability to organize. We call upon you to support legislation that protects these rights and to stand against any forces that seek to undermine them.

In this critical juncture, we also emphasize the importance of international solidarity among workers. The struggles faced by laborers in one country resonate with those in another. The fight against oppression is a universal endeavor, and we must unite to confront the challenges that lie ahead.

We hope that your administration will heed the voices of the working class and take bold actions to ensure justice and equality for all. The future of your nation and the world depends on the recognition of the inherent dignity of every individual.

In solidarity,

The Working Men's International Association

# International Working Men's Association 1865

## Introduction

The International Working Men's Association, also known as the First International, was founded in 1864. It aimed to unite various socialist, communist, and labor groups across Europe and beyond. The organization sought to promote the interests of the working class and to advocate for their rights.

## Objectives

The primary objectives of the International Working Men's Association included:

1. The promotion of international solidarity among workers.
   
2. The establishment of a cooperative society based on the common ownership of the means of production.

3. The advocacy for political rights and social reforms to improve the conditions of the working class.

## Structure

The Association was structured to include various national sections, each representing the interests of workers in their respective countries. These sections were encouraged to communicate and collaborate, sharing strategies and experiences.

## Key Figures

Prominent figures in the International Working Men's Association included Karl Marx, who played a significant role in its formation and development. Other notable members included Mikhail Bakunin and Ferdinand Lassalle, each contributing their perspectives on socialism and labor rights.

## Achievements

The International Working Men's Association successfully organized several congresses, where workers from different nations gathered to discuss their struggles and strategies. These congresses helped to raise awareness of labor issues and fostered a sense of unity among workers worldwide.

## Conclusion

The International Working Men's Association laid the groundwork for future labor movements and socialist organizations. Its emphasis on international solidarity and collective action continues to inspire workers' rights movements to this day.

content:
# To the Working Men of Great Britain and Ireland 1865

## Introduction

Working men of Great Britain and Ireland! 

The time has come for you to unite and take action. The struggle for your rights has been long and arduous, but it is a struggle that must continue until victory is achieved. 

## The Importance of Unity

You must stand together, for divided you will fall. The interests of the working class are the same, and only through solidarity can you hope to achieve your goals. 

Remember, "An injury to one is an injury to all." Your strength lies in your numbers, and together you can demand justice and equality.

## The Role of the State

The state has often been an instrument of oppression, serving the interests of the ruling class. It is essential that you recognize this and work to change the system from within. 

You must strive for a government that represents the will of the people, not just the wealthy elite. 

## The Call to Action

Now is the time to act! Organize, educate, and mobilize your fellow workers. 

Demand better wages, better working conditions, and the right to a voice in the political arena. 

You have the power to change your circumstances, but it requires determination and courage. 

## Conclusion

In closing, remember that the fight for your rights is not just a struggle for today, but for future generations. 

Stand firm in your beliefs, support one another, and never lose sight of the goal: a fair and just society for all working men and women. 

Together, you can achieve greatness.

# Record of the Central Council Meeting

## Introduction

The Central Council convened on the 1st of January, 1864, to discuss the pressing issues facing the working class and the future of the International Workingmen's Association.

## Agenda

The agenda included the following key points:

1. The establishment of the International Workingmen's Association.
2. The role of the working class in the current political landscape.
3. Strategies for uniting workers across national boundaries.

## Establishment of the International Workingmen's Association

The formation of the International Workingmen's Association is a significant step towards uniting the working class. It aims to provide a platform for workers to voice their concerns and organize collectively against exploitation.

The Council emphasized the importance of solidarity among workers from different countries. "Workers of the world, unite!" must be our rallying cry as we face the challenges posed by capitalism.

## Role of the Working Class

The working class is not merely a passive entity; it is the driving force of societal change. The Council discussed how the working class must take an active role in shaping political discourse and policy.

It was noted that the bourgeoisie seeks to divide workers based on nationality, race, and other factors. The Council urged members to resist these divisive tactics and to promote unity among all workers.

## Strategies for Uniting Workers

To effectively unite workers, the Council proposed several strategies:

- Establishing communication channels between different national organizations.
- Organizing international conferences to discuss common issues.
- Promoting educational initiatives to raise awareness about workers' rights and struggles.

The Council recognized that the path to unity would not be easy, but it is essential for the advancement of the working class.

## Conclusion

The meeting concluded with a renewed commitment to the principles of the International Workingmen's Association. The Council called upon all members to actively participate in the movement and to work towards a future where workers are no longer oppressed by the capitalist system. 

Together, we can forge a new path towards justice and equality for all workers.

# International Working Men's Association 1866

## Introduction

The International Working Men's Association (IWMA) was founded in 1864 in London. It aimed to unite various working-class movements across Europe and beyond, promoting the interests of the working class and advocating for social change.

## Objectives

The primary objectives of the IWMA included:

1. **Unity of the Working Class**: To bring together workers from different countries to form a united front against capitalist exploitation.

2. **Advocacy for Workers' Rights**: To promote legislation that would improve working conditions, secure fair wages, and establish rights for workers.

3. **International Solidarity**: To foster a sense of solidarity among workers worldwide, recognizing that the struggles of one country were interconnected with those of others.

## Key Principles

The IWMA was guided by several key principles:

- **Collective Action**: The belief that workers could achieve their goals through collective action and organization.

- **Political Engagement**: The necessity of engaging in political processes to effect change, including the support of political parties that represented workers' interests.

- **Education and Awareness**: The importance of educating workers about their rights and the nature of capitalist exploitation.

## Achievements

The IWMA had several notable achievements during its existence:

- **Formation of Local Sections**: The establishment of local sections in various countries, which helped to organize workers and spread the message of the association.

- **International Conferences**: The organization of international conferences that brought together workers from different nations to discuss common issues and strategies.

- **Influence on Labor Movements**: The IWMA played a significant role in influencing labor movements and socialist parties around the world.

## Conclusion

The International Working Men's Association laid the groundwork for future labor movements and international solidarity among workers. Its legacy continues to inspire contemporary struggles for workers' rights and social justice.

content:
# Survey of the Progress of The International

## Introduction

The International Workingmen's Association, commonly known as the First International, was founded in 1864. It emerged as a response to the growing discontent among workers in the face of industrial capitalism. The organization aimed to unite workers across national boundaries to fight for their rights and improve their conditions.

## The Formation of The International

The formation of The International was a significant milestone in the history of the labor movement. It brought together various socialist and labor groups under a common banner. The founding congress in London marked the beginning of a new era in the struggle for workers' rights.

The International sought to address the issues faced by workers, including exploitation, poor working conditions, and lack of political representation. It aimed to create solidarity among workers of different nations, emphasizing that their struggles were interconnected.

## The Role of Marx

Karl Marx played a crucial role in the development of The International. His theories on class struggle and historical materialism provided a foundation for the organization's principles. Marx's ideas emphasized the importance of collective action and the need for workers to unite against their oppressors.

Marx's influence was evident in the resolutions and statements issued by The International. His writings inspired many workers and activists, encouraging them to take action against the injustices they faced.

## Achievements and Challenges

The International achieved several notable successes during its early years. It organized strikes, supported workers' rights, and promoted socialist ideas across Europe. The organization also facilitated communication and cooperation among various labor groups.

However, The International faced significant challenges as well. Internal divisions arose due to differing ideologies and strategies among its members. The tensions between anarchists and Marxists, in particular, threatened the unity of the organization.

Despite these challenges, The International continued to grow and adapt. It became a platform for workers to voice their concerns and advocate for change. The organization laid the groundwork for future labor movements and socialist organizations.

## Conclusion

The progress of The International marked a pivotal moment in the history of the labor movement. It united workers across borders and provided a framework for collective action. The ideas and principles established by The International continue to resonate in contemporary struggles for workers' rights and social justice.

The legacy of The International serves as a reminder of the power of solidarity and the importance of fighting for a fair and just society.

# The International Workingmen’s Association

## Instructions for the Delegates of the Provisional General Council

The Provisional General Council has resolved to send delegates to the various countries in order to organize the working class and to promote the interests of the International Workingmen’s Association. 

The delegates are entrusted with the task of disseminating the principles of the International, as well as gathering information regarding the conditions of the working class in their respective countries. 

It is essential that the delegates maintain a clear understanding of the objectives of the International and the necessity of solidarity among workers across national boundaries. 

The delegates must engage with local labor organizations and encourage them to join the International. They should also work to establish connections with other social movements that align with the goals of the International. 

## Responsibilities of the Delegates

1. **Promotion of the International’s Principles**: The delegates should actively promote the foundational principles of the International, emphasizing the importance of class struggle and the need for collective action among workers.

2. **Gathering Information**: It is crucial for delegates to collect data on the conditions of the working class in their countries. This information will be vital for the development of strategies to improve the situation of workers.

3. **Building Solidarity**: The delegates must foster a spirit of solidarity among workers. They should encourage collaboration between different labor organizations and promote joint actions.

4. **Reporting Back**: Delegates are expected to report back to the Provisional General Council on their activities, the state of the working class, and any significant developments in their countries.

## Conclusion

The work of the delegates is of utmost importance for the success of the International Workingmen’s Association. By organizing the working class and promoting solidarity, they will contribute to the advancement of the workers’ movement on a global scale. 

The Provisional General Council trusts that the delegates will carry out their responsibilities with dedication and commitment to the cause of the working class.

Their commitment to the cause of labor has not gone unnoticed, and their contributions have laid the groundwork for future advancements in workers' rights.

The discussions and resolutions that emerged from this Congress reflect the collective aspirations of workers worldwide. They serve as a testament to the power of solidarity and the importance of international cooperation in the fight against exploitation and oppression.

We recognize the challenges faced by the delegates in their pursuit of justice for the working class. Their courage and determination in the face of adversity inspire us all to continue the struggle for a more equitable society.

In conclusion, we reaffirm our support for the Central (General) Council and its delegates. We stand united in our commitment to the principles of socialism and the fight for a better future for all workers. Let us carry forward the spirit of Geneva and work together to achieve our common goals.

# On The Lausanne Congress 1867

The Lausanne Congress of 1867 was a significant event in the history of the international workers' movement. It marked a turning point in the organization and direction of socialist and labor movements across Europe. 

The Congress brought together various factions and groups, each with their own ideologies and goals. The debates that took place were intense and often contentious, reflecting the diverse perspectives within the movement. 

## The Context of the Congress

The backdrop of the Lausanne Congress was the rapidly changing political landscape of Europe. The rise of industrial capitalism had created new social classes and heightened class struggles. Workers were beginning to organize themselves in response to the exploitation they faced in factories and urban centers.

In this context, the Congress aimed to unite different socialist factions under a common banner, promoting solidarity among workers across national borders. 

## Key Themes and Discussions

One of the central themes of the Congress was the question of political action versus trade union activity. Delegates debated whether the focus should be on achieving political power through elections or on improving conditions for workers through direct action and strikes.

Another important discussion revolved around the role of the state in the lives of workers. Some delegates argued for a revolutionary approach to dismantling the capitalist state, while others believed in reforming it from within.

## Outcomes of the Congress

The Lausanne Congress resulted in several important resolutions that aimed to strengthen the international workers' movement. It called for the establishment of a more coordinated approach to organizing workers and emphasized the need for international solidarity.

The Congress also highlighted the necessity of education and political consciousness among the working class. It recognized that for workers to effectively challenge capitalism, they must be informed and organized.

In conclusion, the Lausanne Congress of 1867 was a pivotal moment in the history of socialism. It laid the groundwork for future international cooperation among workers and set the stage for the ongoing struggles against capitalism. The debates and resolutions from this Congress continue to resonate in contemporary discussions about labor and socialism.

# The International Workingmen's Association, Resolutions concerning the agenda of the Lausanne Congress

## Resolution on the Political Situation

The political situation in various countries has reached a critical point. The working class must unite and take action to address the injustices faced by the proletariat. 

It is essential to recognize that the struggles of workers are interconnected across borders. The bourgeoisie seeks to divide us, but we must stand together in solidarity.

## Resolution on Economic Conditions

The economic conditions of the working class continue to deteriorate. Wages are stagnant, and the cost of living is rising. 

We call for immediate measures to improve the economic situation of workers. This includes demands for higher wages, better working conditions, and the right to organize.

## Resolution on International Solidarity

International solidarity is crucial for the success of the working class movement. We must support our comrades in other countries who are fighting against oppression and exploitation. 

The International Workingmen's Association must strengthen its ties with other labor organizations globally. Together, we can create a powerful force for change.

## Resolution on Education and Awareness

Education is a vital tool in the struggle for workers' rights. We must educate our members about the principles of socialism and the importance of collective action. 

We propose the establishment of educational programs that focus on the history of the labor movement and the theory of Marxism. 

By raising awareness, we can empower workers to take action and demand their rights.

## Conclusion

The resolutions presented at the Lausanne Congress are a call to action for all workers. We must unite, educate ourselves, and fight for a better future. 

The time for change is now, and together we can achieve our goals.

content:
# The International Workingmen's Association

## Resolution on Attitude to the Congress of the League of Peace and Freedom

The International Workingmen's Association, representing the interests of the working class, acknowledges the necessity of addressing the issues of peace and freedom in the context of the ongoing struggles faced by laborers worldwide. 

The Congress of the League of Peace and Freedom presents an opportunity to engage with various factions advocating for peace. However, it is imperative to critically assess the underlying motives and implications of such a congress. 

The working class must remain vigilant against any attempts to co-opt their struggles for peace into a framework that does not prioritize their rights and needs. 

In this regard, the International Workingmen's Association resolves to participate in the Congress of the League of Peace and Freedom with the following stipulations:

1. **Promotion of Workers' Rights**: Any discourse on peace must be intrinsically linked to the promotion of workers' rights. The fight for peace cannot be separated from the fight for social justice, and the dignity of labor must be at the forefront of any discussions.

2. **Critique of Militarism**: The Association will actively critique any militaristic undertones present in the discussions. True peace cannot be achieved while the specter of war looms over the working class, and militarism must be denounced in all its forms.

3. **Solidarity with Oppressed Peoples**: The International Workingmen's Association will express solidarity with all oppressed peoples globally. The struggle for peace must encompass the fight against imperialism and colonialism, which disproportionately affect the working class.

4. **Advocacy for International Cooperation**: The Association will advocate for genuine international cooperation among workers of all nations. Peace cannot be achieved in isolation; it requires a united front against the forces of exploitation and oppression.

In conclusion, the International Workingmen's Association will approach the Congress of the League of Peace and Freedom with a critical eye, ensuring that the voices of the working class are heard and that their struggles are not sidelined in the pursuit of a superficial peace. 

The resolution is adopted with the understanding that the fight for peace is inextricably linked to the fight for the rights and dignity of all workers.

# The International Workingmen's Association, On the Fenian Prisoners in Manchester

The International Workingmen's Association, representing the working class of various nations, expresses its solidarity with the Fenian prisoners in Manchester. These men, who have fought for the liberation of their homeland, are now suffering under the oppressive hand of British imperialism.

The plight of the Fenian prisoners is not just a matter of national concern; it is a matter of class struggle. The working class must unite across borders to support those who are imprisoned for their beliefs and actions against tyranny. The struggle for Irish independence is intertwined with the broader struggle against capitalist oppression.

## The Role of the Working Class

The working class has a vital role to play in the fight for justice. It is essential that we recognize our shared interests and stand together against our common oppressors. The Fenian prisoners represent the courage and determination of the Irish people, and their struggle is a reflection of the struggles faced by workers everywhere.

We must not forget that the fight for freedom is a fight for all oppressed peoples. The British state seeks to divide us, to pit one group against another, but we must resist this tactic. Solidarity among the working class is our strongest weapon against exploitation and oppression.

## Call to Action

We call upon all workers, regardless of nationality, to demand the release of the Fenian prisoners. Let us raise our voices in unison to condemn the injustices they face. We must organize protests, write letters, and mobilize our communities to show that we stand with our brothers and sisters in their time of need.

In this moment, we have the opportunity to demonstrate our commitment to the principles of international solidarity. Let us not shy away from this responsibility. The fight for the Fenian prisoners is a fight for the dignity of all workers.

Together, we can make a difference. Together, we can show that the spirit of the working class knows no borders. Let us unite in our struggle for justice and freedom for all.

# The Geneva Lock-Out

## Introduction

The Geneva lock-out represents a significant episode in the labor struggles of the late 19th century. It illustrates the tensions between capital and labor, highlighting the strategies employed by both sides in the pursuit of their interests.

## Background

In the spring of 1878, the Geneva watchmakers found themselves embroiled in a conflict that would have lasting implications for labor relations in Switzerland. The watchmakers, skilled artisans, were facing increasing pressure from manufacturers who sought to reduce costs and maximize profits.

The manufacturers, driven by the imperatives of capital accumulation, implemented a series of measures aimed at undermining the workers' rights. This included wage cuts and the introduction of piecework, which fragmented the workforce and diminished collective bargaining power.

## The Lock-Out

In response to these provocations, the watchmakers organized a strike to demand fair wages and better working conditions. The manufacturers, however, retaliated with a lock-out, effectively shutting down the industry and leaving the workers without income.

This lock-out was not merely a tactical maneuver; it was a declaration of war against the organized labor movement. The manufacturers aimed to break the spirit of the workers and demonstrate their power over the labor force.

## The Struggle

As the lock-out continued, the solidarity among the workers grew stronger. They organized mutual aid societies and sought support from other labor organizations. The struggle became a rallying point for workers across Switzerland, who recognized the importance of standing together against exploitation.

Despite the hardships faced during the lock-out, the workers remained resolute. They understood that their fight was not only for their immediate needs but also for the future of labor rights in their country.

## Conclusion

The Geneva lock-out serves as a powerful reminder of the ongoing struggle between capital and labor. It highlights the necessity for workers to unite and resist the encroachments of capital. The lessons learned from this episode continue to resonate in contemporary labor movements, underscoring the importance of solidarity and collective action in the face of adversity.

content:
# On the Consequences of Using Machinery under Capitalism

## Introduction

In this speech, I aim to address the implications of machinery within the capitalist system. The introduction of machinery has transformed the labor process, but it has also led to significant consequences for workers and society as a whole.

## The Role of Machinery

Machinery serves as a tool for increasing productivity. However, it is essential to recognize that this increase in productivity does not benefit the workers. Instead, it serves the interests of capitalists who seek to maximize profits.

The introduction of machinery leads to the displacement of labor. Workers find themselves replaced by machines, which can perform tasks more efficiently. This displacement creates a surplus of labor, leading to unemployment and underemployment.

## The Impact on Labor

The use of machinery alters the nature of work. Workers are no longer skilled artisans; they become mere appendages to machines. This de-skilling of labor results in a loss of craftsmanship and individuality.

Moreover, the reliance on machinery creates a rhythm of work that is dictated by the machine rather than the worker. This alienation from the labor process further exacerbates the plight of the working class.

## Capitalist Exploitation

Capitalists exploit the increased productivity generated by machinery to extract more surplus value from workers. The profits gained from this exploitation are not shared with the labor force but are instead reinvested to further enhance machinery and increase capital.

This cycle perpetuates the inequality inherent in the capitalist system. As machinery becomes more advanced, the gap between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat widens.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, while machinery has the potential to enhance productivity, its use under capitalism leads to significant social and economic consequences. The displacement of labor, the de-skilling of workers, and the exploitation of surplus value are all critical issues that must be addressed.

The struggle for workers' rights must include a critique of the role of machinery in the capitalist system. Only through collective action can we hope to reclaim the dignity of labor and ensure that the benefits of productivity are equitably distributed.

# On the Successes of The International in Germany and France

## Speech by Karl Marx, 1868

Comrades,

The successes of the International Workingmen's Association in Germany and France are not merely the result of our efforts; they are the fruits of the struggles of the working class itself. It is the consciousness of the workers that has awakened, and they are now ready to fight for their rights.

In Germany, we have seen the emergence of a powerful movement that unites workers across various industries. This movement is not just a reaction to the economic conditions but a profound realization of the need for solidarity among the proletariat. The workers are beginning to understand that their liberation is tied to the liberation of all workers worldwide.

In France, the situation is equally promising. The workers have taken to the streets, demonstrating their strength and determination. They are no longer willing to accept the status quo. The revolutionary spirit is alive, and it is inspiring workers in other countries to rise against their oppressors.

The International has played a crucial role in these developments. It has provided a platform for workers to share their experiences and strategies. Through this organization, we have been able to coordinate our efforts and amplify our voices. The unity of the working class is our greatest weapon against the capitalist system.

However, we must remain vigilant. The ruling classes will not relinquish their power without a fight. They will use every means at their disposal to suppress our movement. We must be prepared to confront these challenges head-on. Our strength lies in our numbers and our unwavering commitment to the cause.

Let us continue to build on our successes. Let us unite workers across borders and strengthen the bonds of solidarity. Together, we can achieve a future free from exploitation and oppression.

In conclusion, the successes of the International in Germany and France are a testament to the power of the working class. We are on the brink of a new era, and it is our duty to seize this moment. Let us march forward with courage and determination.

Thank you.

content:
# Speech by Karl Marx 1868

## Introduction

Comrades, I stand before you today to discuss the pressing issues of our time. The struggles of the working class are not merely local phenomena; they are part of a larger, global movement. 

The capitalist system has created a world where the few thrive at the expense of the many. It is our duty to analyze this system critically and to understand the forces that shape our lives.

## The Nature of Capitalism

Capitalism is characterized by the private ownership of the means of production. This ownership leads to the exploitation of labor, as workers are compelled to sell their labor for wages that are far less than the value they produce.

The capitalist seeks to maximize profit, often at the expense of the worker's well-being. This creates a fundamental contradiction within the system: while the capitalist accumulates wealth, the worker remains impoverished.

## The Role of the Working Class

The working class is the backbone of society. Without our labor, the capitalist system would collapse. It is essential for us to recognize our power and to unite in our struggle for better conditions.

We must organize and fight for our rights. The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles. 

## Conclusion

In conclusion, we must remain vigilant and committed to our cause. The fight for justice and equality is ongoing, and it requires our collective strength. 

Let us move forward together, united in our struggle against oppression and exploitation. The future belongs to the working class!

# The International Workingmen's Association, On the Dissolution of the Lassallean Workers' Association

The dissolution of the Lassallean Workers' Association marks a significant moment in the history of the labor movement. It is essential to understand the implications of this event for the future of the working class and the broader socialist movement.

The Lassallean movement, founded by Ferdinand Lassalle, aimed to unite the working class under a single banner. However, it became clear that the principles guiding this association were fundamentally flawed. Lassalle's approach emphasized the role of the state and sought to achieve social reforms through political means, rather than through the direct action of the workers themselves.

## The Limitations of Lassallean Thought

Lassalle's reliance on the state as a vehicle for change led to a number of critical shortcomings. Firstly, it underestimated the power of the capitalist class and the inherent contradictions within the capitalist system. The state, as it existed, was not a neutral arbiter but a tool of the ruling class, serving to maintain the status quo rather than to liberate the working class.

Secondly, the Lassallean focus on political engagement diverted attention from the need for grassroots organization and direct action among workers. The belief that political power could be seized through electoral means alone was a dangerous illusion that ultimately weakened the revolutionary potential of the working class.

## The Path Forward

In light of these failures, it is imperative for the working class to forge a new path. The dissolution of the Lassallean Workers' Association should serve as a catalyst for re-evaluating our strategies and tactics. The future of the labor movement lies not in seeking alliances with the state, but in building a robust, independent workers' movement that is capable of challenging the capitalist system from the ground up.

This requires a renewed commitment to international solidarity among workers. The struggles of the working class are interconnected across borders, and only through unity can we hope to achieve meaningful change. The International Workingmen's Association stands as a testament to this principle, advocating for the rights and dignity of workers everywhere.

In conclusion, the dissolution of the Lassallean Workers' Association is not an end but a beginning. It is an opportunity for the working class to reflect on past mistakes and to chart a new course towards liberation. The path may be fraught with challenges, but with determination and solidarity, we can build a future that honors the struggles of those who came before us.

content:
# On the Condition of the Coalminers in Saxony

## Speech by Karl Marx, 1868

The condition of the coalminers in Saxony is a subject that demands our attention. It is not merely a question of labor; it is a question of humanity. The miners are subjected to a life of hardship, danger, and degradation, which is a direct consequence of the capitalist mode of production.

The miners work long hours in perilous conditions. They descend into the depths of the earth, where they are exposed to the constant threat of accidents. The mines are dark, damp, and filled with toxic gases. The workers are often forced to work in silence, as the roar of machinery drowns out their cries for help.

The wages paid to the miners are insufficient to support their families. They are often paid in scrip, which can only be used at company stores, where prices are inflated. This system of payment keeps the miners in a state of perpetual debt and dependency.

Moreover, the health of the miners is severely compromised. The dust and fumes they inhale lead to chronic respiratory diseases. Many miners do not live to see old age, as their bodies are worn down by the relentless demands of their labor.

The plight of the coalminers is a reflection of the broader injustices inherent in capitalism. Their struggle is not just for better wages or safer working conditions; it is a struggle for dignity and respect. The miners are not merely cogs in a machine; they are human beings deserving of a life free from exploitation.

In conclusion, we must stand in solidarity with the coalminers of Saxony. Their fight is our fight. We must advocate for their rights and work towards a system that values human life over profit. Only then can we hope to create a society where all workers can thrive.

# The International Workingmen's Association

## The Right of Inheritance

The right of inheritance is a crucial aspect of the capitalist system. It allows the wealthy to pass on their fortunes to their descendants, perpetuating inequality and class divisions. This practice ensures that wealth remains concentrated in the hands of a few, while the majority of the population struggles to make ends meet.

Inheritance is not merely a personal matter; it has profound social implications. When wealth is inherited, it creates a class of people who have not earned their wealth but benefit from it nonetheless. This leads to a society where privilege is inherited rather than earned, undermining the principles of meritocracy and equality.

Furthermore, the right of inheritance contributes to the perpetuation of capitalist exploitation. The wealthy use their inherited fortunes to invest in businesses and properties, further increasing their wealth and power. This cycle of wealth accumulation creates a barrier for the working class, making it difficult for them to ascend the social ladder.

The International Workingmen's Association advocates for the abolition of the right of inheritance. By eliminating this practice, we can begin to dismantle the structures of inequality that have been built over generations. The wealth of society should be distributed equitably, ensuring that all individuals have the opportunity to thrive, regardless of their background.

In conclusion, the right of inheritance is a fundamental issue that must be addressed in the struggle for social justice. By challenging this practice, we can work towards a more equitable society where wealth is not concentrated in the hands of a few, but shared among all.

# The International Workingmen's Association, Letter to the Beobachter

To the Editor of the Beobachter,

The International Workingmen's Association, representing the interests of the working class across various nations, wishes to address the recent developments concerning the labor movement and the political landscape that affects our members.

We have observed with great concern the growing divide between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. The interests of the working class are increasingly marginalized, and the need for solidarity among workers of all nations has never been more pressing. 

## The Role of the Proletariat

The proletariat must recognize its strength and potential as a revolutionary force. It is essential for workers to unite, not only within their own countries but also across borders. The struggles of the working class are interconnected, and only through collective action can we hope to achieve meaningful change.

The bourgeoisie seeks to maintain its power by sowing division among workers. It is our duty to resist these tactics and to forge alliances that transcend national boundaries. 

## Call to Action

We urge all workers to engage in political activism and to support organizations that advocate for labor rights. The fight for better working conditions, fair wages, and social justice is a fight for our dignity and future.

Let us stand together in solidarity, for the liberation of the working class is the liberation of all humanity. 

In unity, we can dismantle the structures of oppression and build a society that values the contributions of every worker. 

Together, we can create a world where justice prevails and the rights of the working class are upheld. 

Yours in solidarity,

The International Workingmen's Association

# Importance and Weakness of English Labour by Marx 1869

The English labour movement has played a significant role in the development of the working class and its struggles. It is characterized by both its strengths and weaknesses, which are essential to understand in the context of the broader social and economic landscape.

## The Importance of English Labour

The English labour movement has been pivotal in shaping the political and social rights of workers. It has contributed to the establishment of trade unions, which have fought for better wages, working conditions, and the right to organize. These unions have become a powerful force in advocating for the interests of the working class.

Moreover, the English labour movement has been instrumental in the development of socialist ideas. It has provided a platform for the dissemination of revolutionary thought and has inspired workers across the globe to fight for their rights. The struggles of English workers have resonated with those in other countries, creating a sense of solidarity among the international working class.

## The Weakness of English Labour

Despite its importance, the English labour movement also exhibits significant weaknesses. One of the primary issues is the fragmentation within the movement itself. Various factions and ideologies often lead to disunity, which undermines the collective strength of the working class. This division can be seen in the differing priorities and strategies among trade unions and political parties.

Additionally, the reliance on parliamentary politics has limited the potential for more radical change. The focus on reformist measures can dilute the revolutionary spirit of the movement, leading to a complacency that hinders the pursuit of more profound social transformation. 

Furthermore, the English labour movement has sometimes failed to adequately address the needs of all workers, particularly marginalized groups. This oversight can create a disconnect between the movement and those it aims to represent, weakening its overall impact.

In conclusion, while the English labour movement has made significant strides in advancing the rights and interests of workers, it must confront its weaknesses to realize its full potential. The interplay between its importance and its shortcomings will continue to shape the future of the working class in England and beyond.

# Works of Karl Marx 1870


## Introduction

The works of Karl Marx from the year 1870 represent a significant period in the development of his theories. This time was marked by a deepening understanding of capitalism and its implications for society. Marx's analysis during this period laid the groundwork for future critiques of political economy.


## The Capitalist Mode of Production

Marx's examination of the capitalist mode of production reveals the inherent contradictions within the system. He argues that capitalism is characterized by the exploitation of labor, where the value produced by workers is appropriated by capitalists. This exploitation leads to class struggle, which is central to Marx's theory of history.


## Historical Materialism

Marx's historical materialism posits that the material conditions of a society's mode of production fundamentally shape its social structures and relations. He emphasizes that history is not a series of isolated events but a complex interplay of economic forces and social relations.


## The Role of Class Struggle

Class struggle is a driving force in Marx's analysis. He asserts that the conflict between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat is the engine of historical change. This struggle is not merely economic but also political and ideological, influencing all aspects of society.


## Conclusion

The works of Karl Marx in 1870 provide critical insights into the nature of capitalism and its effects on society. His theories continue to resonate, offering a framework for understanding the dynamics of class, power, and economic relations in the modern world.

- It fostered a sense of international solidarity among workers, leading to cross-border cooperation.


## Conclusion


The International Workingmen's Association laid the groundwork for future labor movements and socialist organizations. Its emphasis on solidarity and collective action continues to inspire workers around the world in their ongoing struggle for rights and justice.

title: Karl Marx in The Times 1871
author: Karl Marx

content:
# Karl Marx in The Times 1871

In the year 1871, Karl Marx's ideas were increasingly becoming a focal point of discussion in various media outlets, including The Times. This period marked a significant evolution in Marxist thought and its reception by the public.

The events of the Paris Commune had a profound impact on Marx's theories. He viewed the Commune as a practical application of his ideas about the dictatorship of the proletariat. In his writings, he emphasized the importance of the working class seizing power and establishing a government that represented their interests.

## The Paris Commune

The Paris Commune was a revolutionary government that ruled Paris from March 18 to May 28, 1871. It was a response to the Franco-Prussian War and the harsh conditions imposed by the German occupation. Marx saw the Commune as a demonstration of the potential for workers to govern themselves.

He argued that the Commune was a "dictatorship of the proletariat" and that it represented a significant step towards the realization of a classless society. Marx believed that the lessons learned from the Commune would be essential for future revolutions.

## The Reception of Marx's Ideas

The reception of Marx's ideas in The Times was mixed. While some articles praised the revolutionary spirit of the Commune, others criticized it as chaotic and misguided. Marx's theories were often misrepresented, leading to misunderstandings about his vision for society.

Despite the criticism, Marx's influence continued to grow. His writings inspired a new generation of socialists and revolutionaries who sought to challenge the status quo. The discussions in The Times reflected a broader societal debate about the role of the working class and the future of capitalism.

In conclusion, the year 1871 was pivotal for Marx and his ideas. The events of the Paris Commune and the subsequent discussions in The Times highlighted the tensions between revolutionary aspirations and the realities of political power. Marx's vision for a just society continued to resonate, shaping the discourse around socialism for years to come.

content:
# International Working Men's Association 1871

## Introduction

The International Working Men's Association, also known as the First International, was founded in 1864. Its purpose was to unite various socialist, communist, and labor groups across Europe and beyond. The association aimed to promote the interests of the working class and advocate for their rights.

## Objectives

The primary objectives of the International Working Men's Association included:

1. Promoting international solidarity among workers.
2. Advocating for the rights and welfare of the working class.
3. Encouraging the establishment of a cooperative society based on common ownership of the means of production.

## Achievements

The International made significant strides in raising awareness about workers' rights and issues. It organized conferences, published pamphlets, and facilitated communication among various labor organizations.

## Challenges

Despite its achievements, the International faced numerous challenges. Internal divisions, differing ideologies, and external pressures from governments hindered its effectiveness. The association struggled to maintain unity among its diverse membership.

## Conclusion

The International Working Men's Association played a crucial role in the early labor movement. Its legacy continues to influence contemporary labor organizations and movements advocating for workers' rights worldwide.

title: Serraillier's report to the International on the events prior to the Commune of Paris, February 1871

content:
# Serraillier's Report to the International on the Events Prior to the Commune of Paris, February 1871

The events leading up to the Commune of Paris in 1871 were marked by a series of significant political and social upheavals. The Franco-Prussian War had left France in a state of turmoil, and the working class was increasingly disillusioned with the existing government. 

The fall of the Second Empire in September 1870 created a power vacuum that various factions sought to fill. The provisional government, established in the wake of the empire's collapse, struggled to maintain control and address the needs of the populace. 

## The Role of the Working Class

The working class played a crucial role in the events that unfolded. As the war dragged on and the situation in Paris deteriorated, workers began to organize themselves into various groups and committees. These organizations sought to address the pressing issues of food shortages, unemployment, and the general state of despair that permeated the city.

The formation of the National Guard was a pivotal moment. It provided a means for the working class to arm themselves and take a stand against the government. The National Guard became a symbol of popular resistance and empowerment, as ordinary citizens took up arms to defend their rights and interests.

## The Siege of Paris

The siege of Paris by Prussian forces exacerbated the already dire conditions. The city was cut off from supplies, leading to widespread hunger and suffering. The provisional government’s inability to effectively respond to the crisis further fueled discontent among the population.

As the siege continued, the spirit of solidarity among the working class grew stronger. They began to see themselves not just as victims of war, but as active participants in shaping their own destiny. This shift in consciousness laid the groundwork for the revolutionary fervor that would erupt in March 1871.

## The Proclamation of the Commune

On March 18, 1871, the people of Paris rose up against the provisional government. The government’s attempt to disarm the National Guard was met with fierce resistance. The insurrection marked the beginning of the Paris Commune, a radical socialist government that aimed to establish a new order based on principles of equality and justice.

The Commune represented a bold experiment in self-governance, with workers taking control of their workplaces and communities. It was a moment of immense hope and possibility, as the ideals of socialism began to take tangible form in the heart of Paris.

## Conclusion

The events leading to the Commune of Paris were a testament to the power of the working class and their desire for change. The struggle for a better society was not just a reaction to the immediate circumstances of war and poverty, but a profound assertion of the rights and dignity of the working people. 

As we reflect on these events, it is essential to recognize the lessons they offer for contemporary struggles. The spirit of the Commune lives on as a reminder of the potential for collective action to challenge oppression and create a more just world.

content:
# The Civil War in France Address of the General Council

## Introduction

The civil war in France is a significant event that has drawn the attention of the working class across the globe. It is essential to analyze this conflict not only as a national struggle but as a pivotal moment in the broader context of the international labor movement.

## The Paris Commune

The Paris Commune represents a bold experiment in the governance of the working class. It emerged from the ashes of the Franco-Prussian War, where the defeat of France ignited a revolutionary spirit among the proletariat. The Commune was a response to the oppressive conditions under the bourgeois government, and it sought to establish a new order based on equality and justice.

The principles of the Commune were rooted in the ideas of democracy and social justice. The workers of Paris aimed to create a society where the needs of the many would take precedence over the profits of the few. They sought to abolish the old order and replace it with a system that reflected the will of the people.

## The Role of the Proletariat

The proletariat played a crucial role in the establishment of the Commune. It was the working class that rose up to challenge the existing power structures and assert their rights. The Commune was a manifestation of their struggle for liberation and self-determination.

The events of the Commune demonstrated the potential of the working class to govern themselves. It showed that the proletariat could organize and implement policies that benefited the majority rather than the elite. This was a significant step towards the realization of a socialist society.

## The Reaction of the Bourgeoisie

The reaction of the bourgeoisie to the Commune was swift and brutal. The ruling class viewed the uprising as a direct threat to their power and privileges. They mobilized their forces to crush the Commune, leading to a violent and bloody repression.

The brutal suppression of the Commune serves as a reminder of the lengths to which the ruling class will go to maintain their dominance. It highlights the inherent conflict between the interests of the bourgeoisie and the aspirations of the working class.

## Conclusion

The civil war in France and the Paris Commune stand as a testament to the struggles of the working class. They illustrate the ongoing fight for justice and equality in the face of oppression. The lessons learned from this period are vital for the continued advancement of the labor movement and the pursuit of a more just society.

The legacy of the Commune lives on, inspiring future generations to challenge the status quo and strive for a world where the rights of the working class are upheld. The struggle continues, and it is imperative that we remain vigilant in our fight for a better future.

# Frederick Engels in The Daily News 1871

## Introduction

In 1871, Frederick Engels contributed to The Daily News, providing insights into the political and social conditions of the time. His writings reflect the struggles of the working class and the implications of the political movements in Europe.

## The Paris Commune

Engels discusses the significance of the Paris Commune, highlighting it as a revolutionary movement that aimed to establish a new social order. He emphasizes the courage and determination of the working class in their fight for liberation.

Engels writes, "The Paris Commune was the first attempt of the working class to take political power." He notes that this event served as a crucial lesson for future revolutionary movements.

## The Role of the State

In his analysis, Engels critiques the existing state structures, arguing that they serve the interests of the ruling class. He asserts that the state must be dismantled to achieve true emancipation for the proletariat.

He states, "The state is nothing more than a machine for the oppression of one class by another." Engels calls for the establishment of a new form of governance that reflects the will of the working class.

## Conclusion

Engels concludes with a call to action for the working class to unite and continue their struggle for a just society. He expresses optimism about the potential for revolutionary change and the eventual triumph of socialism.

He urges, "Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains." This rallying cry encapsulates the spirit of the time and the enduring fight for equality and justice.

content:
# Resolution on Working Class Political Action by International Working Men's Association September 1871

The General Council of the International Working Men’s Association, assembled in London, has deemed it necessary to express its views on the political action of the working class.

The working class must organize itself as a political party, independent of all existing political parties. It must strive for the emancipation of the working class, which can only be achieved through the overthrow of the capitalist system.

## The Necessity of Political Action

The working class cannot rely on the goodwill of the ruling classes. It must take its destiny into its own hands. Political action is essential for the working class to achieve its aims. This action must be based on the principles of solidarity and unity among workers.

The political struggle is not merely a struggle for better wages or working conditions; it is a struggle for the complete liberation of the working class from the chains of capitalism.

## The Role of the International

The International Working Men’s Association has an important role to play in this political struggle. It must serve as a platform for the working class to unite and coordinate its efforts across national boundaries. 

The International must promote the idea that the interests of the working class are universal and that workers of all countries must stand together against their common oppressors.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the working class must recognize the necessity of political action and the importance of organizing itself as a distinct political force. The struggle for the emancipation of the working class is a political struggle that requires unity, solidarity, and a clear understanding of the goals to be achieved.

The General Council calls upon all workers to join in this struggle and to work towards the establishment of a society based on equality and justice for all.

content:
# General Rules of the International Working Men's Association


## Section 1: Name

The name of the Association shall be the International Working Men's Association.


## Section 2: Purpose

The purpose of the Association is to promote the interests of the working class and to unite workers of all countries in the struggle for their rights.


## Section 3: Membership

Membership is open to all workers, regardless of nationality, race, or religion, who accept the principles of the Association.


## Section 4: Organization

The Association shall be organized on a federal basis, with local sections in each country and a central governing body.


## Section 5: Responsibilities

Members are expected to actively participate in the activities of the Association and to support its objectives.


## Section 6: Meetings

Regular meetings shall be held to discuss issues affecting workers and to plan actions to promote their interests.


## Section 7: Amendments

Amendments to these rules may be proposed by any member and shall be adopted by a two-thirds majority of the members present at a meeting.


## Section 8: Dissolution

The Association may be dissolved by a two-thirds majority vote of the members, provided that notice of the proposal to dissolve has been given at least one month in advance.

# Works of Frederick Engels 1871

## Introduction

The works of Frederick Engels, a prominent figure in the development of Marxist theory, provide critical insights into the social, political, and economic structures of his time. Engels collaborated closely with Karl Marx, and together they laid the foundations for modern socialism and communism.

## The Condition of the Working Class in England

In this seminal work, Engels examines the dire circumstances faced by the working class in England during the Industrial Revolution. He highlights the exploitation and degradation of workers, emphasizing the need for social reform.

Engels writes, "The condition of the working class is a reflection of the capitalist system, which prioritizes profit over human dignity."

## The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State

In this text, Engels explores the historical development of family structures, property rights, and state power. He argues that these institutions are not natural but rather products of specific historical conditions.

Engels asserts, "The family, as we know it today, is a product of the economic relations of the time."

## Anti-Dühring

Engels critiques the ideas of Eugen Dühring, a contemporary philosopher, in this comprehensive work. He defends the principles of scientific socialism against Dühring's revisionist theories.

Engels states, "Scientific socialism is rooted in the materialist conception of history."

## The Role of Labor in the Transition from Ape to Man

In this essay, Engels discusses the significance of labor in human evolution. He posits that the development of tools and the division of labor were pivotal in shaping human society.

Engels emphasizes, "It is through labor that humanity has transformed nature and itself."

## Conclusion

The writings of Frederick Engels remain relevant today, as they provide a critical lens through which to analyze contemporary social issues. His work continues to inspire movements for social justice and equality around the world.

title: Works Frederick Engels 1872

content:
# Works of Frederick Engels 1872

## Introduction

In the year 1872, the works of Frederick Engels were published, contributing significantly to the development of Marxist theory. Engels, alongside Karl Marx, laid the foundations for a scientific understanding of society, economics, and history.

## The Role of Labor in the Development of Society

Labor is the primary factor in the development of society. It is through labor that humans transform nature and create the conditions for their existence. The evolution of labor has led to the formation of different social structures, each characterized by its own mode of production.

## Historical Materialism

Historical materialism is the methodology used by Marx and Engels to analyze the development of human societies. It posits that the material conditions of a society's mode of production fundamentally determine its organization and development. 

### The Base and Superstructure

The relationship between the economic base and the ideological superstructure is crucial in understanding societal changes. The base consists of the forces and relations of production, while the superstructure includes culture, ideology, and politics. Changes in the economic base lead to transformations in the superstructure.

## Class Struggle

Class struggle is the driving force of historical development. Throughout history, different classes have emerged, each with conflicting interests. The struggle between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat is the most significant in modern society, as it shapes the political landscape and influences social change.

## Conclusion

Engels' contributions to Marxist theory remain relevant today. His analysis of labor, historical materialism, and class struggle provides a framework for understanding contemporary social issues. The works of Engels continue to inspire movements for social justice and equality around the world.

content:
# Works of Frederick Engels 1873

## Introduction

The works of Frederick Engels are a cornerstone of Marxist theory and provide essential insights into the development of socialist thought. Engels, alongside Karl Marx, laid the foundations for a scientific understanding of society, economics, and politics.

## The Condition of the Working Class in England

Engels's seminal work, "The Condition of the Working Class in England," examines the dire circumstances faced by the proletariat during the Industrial Revolution. He meticulously details the living conditions, labor exploitation, and social injustices that characterized this period.

Engels argues that the capitalist system inherently leads to the degradation of the working class. He writes, "The capitalist mode of production is based on the exploitation of labor, and this exploitation is the root of all social evils."

## Socialism: Utopian and Scientific

In "Socialism: Utopian and Scientific," Engels distinguishes between utopian socialism and scientific socialism. He critiques the former for its idealistic nature and emphasizes the importance of a materialist approach to social change.

Engels states, "Scientific socialism is grounded in the realities of class struggle and the material conditions of society. It is not merely a dream of a better world but a practical guide to achieving it."

## The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State

In this work, Engels explores the historical development of the family, private property, and the state. He argues that these institutions are products of specific economic conditions and serve to perpetuate class oppression.

Engels asserts, "The family, as we know it today, is a social construct that has evolved alongside the rise of private property and class society."

## Conclusion

Engels's writings remain relevant today as they provide a critical lens through which to analyze contemporary social issues. His emphasis on class struggle and the material conditions of life continues to inspire activists and scholars alike. 

Through his works, Engels invites us to understand the world not as it is, but as it could be through collective action and revolutionary change.

content:
# Proclamation on Dissolution of the International Workingmen's Association 1876

The International Workingmen's Association, founded in 1864, has served as a vital platform for the working class across nations. However, after careful consideration and in light of recent developments, it has become necessary to announce the dissolution of this esteemed organization.

The challenges faced by the Association have grown insurmountable. Internal divisions, differing political ideologies, and the rise of nationalist sentiments have weakened our collective strength. The unity that once characterized our movement has been compromised, making it increasingly difficult to pursue our common goals.

## The Need for Dissolution

The decision to dissolve the International Workingmen's Association is not taken lightly. It is a recognition of the current realities that confront us. The fragmentation of our movement has hindered our ability to effectively advocate for the rights and interests of the working class.

In recent years, we have witnessed a shift in focus among various factions within the Association. Some have prioritized national interests over international solidarity, undermining the very foundation upon which we were built. This divergence has led to a lack of coherence in our strategies and objectives.

## A Call for New Beginnings

While the dissolution of the International Workingmen's Association marks the end of an era, it also opens the door for new beginnings. It is imperative that we learn from our past experiences and seek to establish new forms of organization that can better address the needs of the working class in today's world.

We must strive to create a movement that transcends borders, one that fosters genuine solidarity among workers everywhere. The fight for social justice, equality, and workers' rights continues, and it is our responsibility to ensure that this struggle is carried forward in a more effective manner.

In conclusion, let us remember the principles that guided the International Workingmen's Association. Let us honor the sacrifices made by countless workers who dedicated their lives to the cause of emancipation. As we move forward, may we do so with renewed determination and a commitment to building a more just and equitable society for all.

title: Moses Kotane
author: Karl Marx
description: Moses Kotane by Karl Marx. Source: Marxists Internet Archive.
content:
# Moses Kotane

Moses Kotane was born at Tamposstad near Rustenberg in the Northern Transvaal in 1905. After only a few years of formal schooling, he worked as a photographer’s assistant, domestic servant, miner and bakery worker. He joined the ANC in 1928 and the Party in 1929. In 1931 he became a full-time functionary of our Party. He was a member of the Bakers’ Trade Union and in 1929 was elected Vice Chairman of the South African Federation of Native Trade Unions. 

In 1931 Kotane joined Albert Nzula as a pupil at the Lenin School in Moscow. When he returned in 1933, Kotane was elected to the Political Bureau of the Party and became its General Secretary in 1939, a position which he held until his death in 1978. In 1943 he served on the ANC Committee which drafted the historic document, African Claims, and in 1948 was elected to the National Executive Committee of the ANC. 

He was arrested in the Defiance Campaign of 1952, the Treason Trial of 1956-61, and the Emergency of 1960. In 1962 he was placed under house arrest. The following year he was sent abroad by the ANC and CP to help organise the external apparatus of the liberation movement. During this period he served as Treasurer-General of the ANC. 

On his 70th birthday he was awarded Isitwalandwe-Seaprankoe and the Soviet Order of the Friendship of the People.
